I advise people who travel to the UK for work, and the question I hear most often is: what am I going to say at the border? My answer is always the same: say less. The officer is going to ask you three things. Why are you here, how long are you staying, and where are you staying. If you are attending a conference, say that, and say when it ends. Do not explain the whole project. Do not mention that the client might offer you a job. The second thing I tell people is to read the fine print of their own plans. Last month a client of mine was flying in for two days of meetings, and then he told me that he was also going to spend a week training the London team. That is work, not a meeting, and it is not a permitted activity for a visitor. So we changed the plan. He will do the training online, from Sao Paulo, next month.

My trip to London is finally confirmed. I'm flying out of Sao Paulo on Sunday night, with a layover in Lisbon, and I land at Heathrow on Monday afternoon. The client is sending a car, so I'm not going to deal with the train and three suitcases. On Tuesday and Wednesday I'm meeting their legal team to negotiate the distribution agreement. If everything goes well, by Thursday evening we will have agreed on every clause except the price, and the price will be the partners' problem, not mine. I applied for my travel authorization six weeks ago, and it came back in two days. I'll be honest: the thing I am most worried about is not the border. It's the jet lag. I always think I will sleep on the plane, and I never do.

First, Pedro checks that his passport will still be valid for the whole trip. Then he applies online for the travel authorization, and it is approved two days later. Next, he asks the client in London for a letter of invitation that describes the meetings. A week before the flight, he prints his itinerary, his return ticket and his proof of funds. Finally, at Heathrow, he tells the border officer that he is attending meetings and flying back on Friday.
